Flag attachments or shared documents that request login before viewing content.

Identify social engineering patterns such as authority pressure (e.g., CEO, professor, IT admin impersonation).
Flag emails that request MFA codes or verification tokens under any circumstance.
Check for poor grammar, unusual tone, or formatting inconsistencies often present in phishing attempts.
Identify “too good to be true” offers such as scholarships, refunds, or rewards requiring action.
Flag emails using generic greetings (e.g., 'Dear user', 'Dear customer') instead of personalized names.
Treat unexpected invoice or payment requests as suspicious unless previously contextualized.
Detect domain spoofing in reply-to headers or mismatched sender display names.
Flag emails instructing users to bypass normal security procedures or ignore warnings.
Identify urgency combined with external links as high-confidence phishing indicators.
